=== CALL C0030 ===
Luke: Hi! Can you hear me alright? I'm Luke.
Debbie: Hello, love, yes, I can hear you lovely. I'm Debbie. Sorry, I've got my glasses right on the end of my nose, I can't see the screen otherwise.
Luke: Ha, no, you're fine. Where are you calling from?
Debbie: Gorleston. That's just by Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, you know, right on the coast.
Luke: Oh, lovely, by the sea. I'm in Bristol. Horfield, up the north side.
Debbie: Bristol, ooh. I've never been, I don't think. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start?
Luke: I did, yeah. I was quite pleased with myself, actually. I think I sort of got into a rhythm with it. How did you get on?
Debbie: Erm, I got about halfway and then Tilly, that's my dog, started barking at the postman, and that was me done, I lost my place completely. So I don't know what I've put, love, honestly.
Luke: That's fair. Postman's a legitimate distraction.
Debbie: That is, that is. Here, I saw your photo, that little drawing of a dog on your shelf. Did one of yours do that?
Luke: Yeah, that's my daughter, Isla. She's nine. She's desperate for a dog, so she draws them instead, kind of as a hint. It's not working yet.
Debbie: Oh bless her. My grandson's four and it's all diggers with him. Diggers, diggers, diggers. He's with me three days a week, and if we go along the seafront and there's roadworks, well, that's the morning gone, we're stood there watching the man in the digger for an hour. Sorry, I've gone off on one, what was I saying?
Luke: No, I love that. Honestly that's a pretty good morning out.
Debbie: Free entertainment, innit. Better than the car park, they've put the charges up again.
Luke: Oh, don't. So are you working, or is it mostly grandson duty?
Debbie: Mostly him now, really. I was on the packing line at a frozen food place near Yarmouth for years, and then they changed the shifts round and I couldn't do it with minding him, so I just sort of... stopped. Two years ago now. I keep saying I'll do a few hours at a charity shop, but I never get round to it, do you know what I mean?
Luke: Yeah, totally. I'm an executive assistant, so I basically run the managing director's diary at an engineering consultancy. Meetings, travel, board stuff, keeping the right people in front of him and the wrong ones away. It sounds dull, but you end up knowing everything that's going on, which I sort of secretly enjoy.
Debbie: Ooh, you're the one in charge really, then.
Luke: Don't tell him that. But, yeah, a bit.
Debbie: My husband Steve's self-employed, he does removals with his van, so there's no diary with him. He just answers the phone and goes. Mind you, the van's just failed its MOT, so he's not going anywhere this week.
Luke: Oh no. That's a pain when it's your living.
Debbie: That is. What do you do when you're not working, then, love?
Luke: Erm, films, mostly. There's a cinema here called the Watershed that does foreign stuff, so I saw a Korean film there last week, which was gorgeous, sort of slow and sad. And I cook a lot. I make my own kimchi, though the last batch went a bit wrong. The whole kitchen smelled of it.
Debbie: Kimchi! I wouldn't know where to start. I'm more of a shepherd's pie girl. And musicals. I've seen Mamma Mia twice, and we do the panto at the Pavilion every year with the grandkids.
Luke: Oh, panto's brilliant, though. I took Isla to the Hippodrome one a couple of years ago and she shouted herself hoarse.
Debbie: That's the best bit, isn't it, the shouting. Oh, he's behind you!
Luke: Exactly. Did you ever think about going on holiday to-

=== CALL C0031 ===
Callum: Hiya, you alright? I'm Callum.
Hira: Hello. Yes, fine, thank you. I'm Hira.
Callum: Nice one. Sorry, I've only just sat back down, I was making a tea. Where abouts are you?
Hira: Reading. Earley, actually, just outside.
Callum: Oh right, yeah. I'm Sittingbourne, in Kent. Not too far, sort of, just the other side of London.
Hira: Okay. I don't know Kent very well. Only passing through, I think.
Callum: Most people only pass through, to be fair. Did you get on alright with the puzzle bit?
Hira: Erm, I think so. I was a bit slow. I like to check things twice, so I didn't finish the last one.
Callum: Yeah, same, I ran out of time on the last one. I was sort of going round in circles. So what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Hira: I work in a hospital pharmacy. On the wards, mostly.
Callum: Oh, nice. That's a proper job, that. That's important stuff.
Hira: It's okay. It's a lot of checking. What about you?
Callum: Erm, I'm a machine operator at a cardboard box place. Corrugated packaging. I run a printer that prints and folds and glues the boxes, and I do the setups when we change orders over. Rotating shifts, so days one week and backs the next. It's not glamorous, but I like it, you know. You know where you are with a machine. Mostly.
Hira: That sounds quite precise, actually. If one setting is wrong, the whole batch is wrong.
Callum: Yeah, exactly that. You do your checks first or you end up with two thousand boxes in the bin. Bit like your job, I suppose, but with nobody getting hurt.
Hira: Yes. We are a bit like that. A small mistake, and then it matters.
Callum: Do you have to get in early and that?
Hira: Before eight, which is the problem, because the car park is a nightmare. If you're five minutes late there's no space at all.
Callum: Oh, I feel that. For me it's the A249. You get one lorry break down and that's it, everyone's sat there.
Hira: Same thing, different road.
Callum: Pretty much, yeah. What do you get up to outside work, then?
Hira: Erm, I walk quite a lot, by the river. I crochet. And I have some plants in pots in the back yard. Chillies, coriander, mint.
Callum: No way, chillies? I grow chillies. I've got raised beds in the garden, I built them myself, and it's tomatoes, chillies and runner beans mostly. How have yours done this year?
Hira: Surprisingly well, actually. I didn't expect it. I think it was the warm few weeks in July.
Callum: That's what I reckon. Mine have gone mad. It's the tomatoes I'm worried about. Half of them are still green and the weather's turning, so it's a bit touch and go, you know.
Hira: My mother-in-law puts the green ones on the windowsill. I think they ripen there.
Callum: Yeah, my mum does that. Only problem is our cat, Biscuit. Anything on the windowsill, he just knocks it straight off. Looks right at you while he does it, too.
Hira: Acha, so the tomatoes are not safe.
Callum: Nothing's safe, mate. Sorry, I mean, nothing is. What sort of chillies have you got, then?
Hira: Erm, just a green one, the small kind. My mum uses them, so I wanted the same. I put them in daal, mostly.
Callum: Oh, that'd be nice. I mostly just chuck mine in a chilli, to be honest. Megan, my wife, says I put too many in, but-

=== CALL C0032 ===
Debbie: Hello, my love! Can you hear me alright? I'm Debbie.
Hira: Hello. Yes, I can hear you. I'm Hira.
Debbie: Oh, that's a lovely name. Sorry, I'm still sat in the kitchen, so you'll have to excuse the mess behind me. The craft box has been out since Tuesday.
Hira: No, it's fine. I saw it in your photo, I think. Is it for cards?
Debbie: That is, yes! Card-making. Well, I say card-making. I've got a whole drawer full of kits I've started and not finished, do you know what I mean? I get to the glitter bit and lose interest.
Hira: I have the same with crochet. I have a blanket that has taken three months.
Debbie: Three months! But at least you're still going with it. What colours?
Hira: Grey and mustard. It's for, erm, just for our sofa, I think. Usually I make small things for colleagues when they have babies. Hats, little blankets.
Debbie: Oh, that's ever so kind. They must love that. Where do you work, then, love?
Hira: At the hospital in Reading. In the pharmacy, on the wards.
Debbie: I said you looked clever, with all them big books behind you. I did, I put that on the form.
Hira: They are mostly heavy, not clever.
Debbie: Do you do the old people's wards and that?
Hira: Yes, quite a lot of the medical wards. Many older patients. Later I'd like to specialise in care of the elderly, maybe.
Debbie: Ah. My mum was in and out of hospital at the end. She had dementia. That's five years ago now. The nurses were lovely with her, they really were. I don't know how you all do it, honestly.
Hira: I'm sorry about your mum. Dementia is very hard. For the families especially.
Debbie: That is. Anyway, sorry, love, I'm going all gloomy on you. Where are you from originally, if you don't mind me asking?
Hira: Pakistan. Faisalabad. I came here seven years ago.
Debbie: Seven years! And do you get back much?
Hira: Once a year, normally, for two or three weeks. My parents are there, and one sister. I talk to my sisters on video at the weekends. Sometimes my sister sends voice notes at three in the morning, our time.
Debbie: Oh, that's the time difference, isn't it! My sister's only round the corner, so she just turns up. I've got nearly all my family within a few miles, you know. I'd be lost without them. Do you miss your mum?
Hira: Yes. More than I say, I think. Mostly I miss her cooking. I'm still trying to make my chapatis as round as hers.
Debbie: Oh, bless you. Mine would come out the shape of Norfolk. What do you cook, then?
Hira: Daal, aloo gosht, mostly Punjabi food. And on Sundays a roast chicken, because my mother-in-law likes it.
Debbie: Ooh, a roast! Do you do Yorkshires?
Hira: Erm, I tried once. They didn't rise. Na, they were flat.
Debbie: That's the oven, love. You want it ever so hot, and the oil smoking before the batter goes in. That's the secret, that is. My Steve won't have a Sunday without them.
Hira: Okay. Very hot. I'll try that. Thank you.
Debbie: And don't open the door! That's where everybody goes wrong, they peek.
Hira: I think I peeked.
Debbie: Everybody does, love. Do you walk at all? I take Tilly, my dog, along the seafront every day. She's got a bad hip, but she still drags me out.
Hira: Yes, I walk by the river on the Thames Path, or round the lake near us. It's nice when it's not raining, which is not often.
Debbie: Oh, the wind off the sea here, that'd take your-

=== CALL C0033 ===
Luke: Hey, Callum, is it? I'm Luke.
Callum: Yeah, that's me. Alright, mate, nice to meet you.
Luke: You too. Where are you?
Callum: Sittingbourne, in Kent. You?
Luke: Bristol. So there's a bit of motorway between us.
Callum: Bit of a trek, yeah. Is that a Studio Ghibli thing behind you? My wife's been on at me to watch one of those.
Luke: It is, yeah, Spirited Away. Oh, you've got to. Start with that one, honestly, or My Neighbour Totoro if you want something gentle. I've got a nine-year-old and she's watched Totoro about forty times.
Callum: Right, I'll tell Megan. She'll be chuffed I've actually remembered something. What do you do, then?
Luke: I'm an exec assistant to the MD at an engineering consultancy. Basically I run his life: diary, board meetings, travel, suppliers. And you?
Callum: Machine operator. Cardboard boxes. I run a flexo printer-folder-gluer, so the board goes in flat and comes out a box, printed and glued. I do the changeovers as well when an order switches. Days one week, backs the next.
Luke: That's actually quite satisfying, isn't it? Like, you can see the thing at the end.
Callum: Yeah, that's it, you can see what you've done. I train the new starters and all, which I quite like. I'm trying to get on the maintenance apprenticeship, so I can fix the machines rather than just run them, you know.
Luke: Oh, nice. That's a smart move. I'm sort of in the same boat, trying to work out the next step. Chief of staff, head of ops, that kind of thing. The trick is making yourself the person nobody can do without, yeah?
Callum: Yeah, I suppose. I just try and do the job properly and hope someone notices.
Luke: That works too, to be fair. Probably more honest than mine. Do you do much sport?
Callum: Five-a-side on Wednesdays with lads from work. I'm at the back, mostly, just stopping people getting through. And I go to Gillingham with my dad now and then.
Luke: Gillingham! I'm Rovers, sort of by inheritance from my dad. I take my daughter a couple of times a season. I'm more of a parkrun person, really. Horfield Common, when she's at her mum's.
Callum: Oh, what do you get round in?
Luke: Erm, on a good day, just under twenty-four. On a bad day I'd rather not say.
Callum: That's decent, that. I'd be dead. I do a bit of cycling on the Saxon Shore Way, but that's about it.
Luke: What do you do when you're not knackered from shifts?
Callum: Garden, mostly. I built raised beds out the back. Tomatoes, chillies, runner beans. I was just talking chillies with Hira in the last one, actually. She grows them too.
Luke: Ha, nice. I make kimchi, so I'm always after chillies. Well, the flakes, gochugaru. My last batch sort of exploded in the jar.
Callum: Exploded?
Luke: Fermentation. The gas builds up. I opened it and it went all up the cupboard. Isla thought it was the best thing ever.
Callum: That's mental. I'm just chilli and fajitas, me. And a kebab on a Friday from the place by the station.
Luke: Honestly, a good kebab's hard to beat. Where've you been on holiday lately? I'm always nosing.
Callum: Lads' weekend in Newcastle last time. And me and Megan do Norfolk or Devon in the summer, a cottage or a caravan. Honeymoon was Crete. I like it all booked and sorted, you know, so nothing goes wrong.
Luke: Oh, you'd be good at my job, then. I did a month in Japan before my daughter came along, and I'm desperate to do Seoul next, but-

=== CALL C0034 ===
Debbie: Hello, love! Ooh, it's you. I said you looked lovely in your photo. I'm Debbie.
Callum: Ha, thank you. Hiya, Debbie, I'm Callum. You alright?
Debbie: I'm fine, love, thank you. Bit worn out with all this talking, I'm not used to it. Where are you, then?
Callum: Sittingbourne, in Kent. Whereabouts are you?
Debbie: Gorleston-on-Sea. Right by Great Yarmouth.
Callum: Oh, no way, we come up to Norfolk most summers, me and my wife. Caravan or a cottage. We did one near Hemsby a couple of years back.
Debbie: Hemsby! That's just up the road, love. Did you get fish and chips on the front?
Callum: Pretty much every night. Megan was like, we can't have chips again, and then we had chips again.
Debbie: That's what you're supposed to do on holiday, that is. We have them every Friday, me and my husband Steve, and we live here.
Callum: Ha. Fair enough. Did you get on alright with the puzzle at the start?
Debbie: Oh, don't. The dog started barking halfway through and I lost my place. What do you do, love?
Callum: I'm a machine operator. I run a printer-folder-gluer at a cardboard box factory. The board goes in flat and comes out a box, basically.
Debbie: Oh, I did packing for years! Frozen food, near Yarmouth. I bet I've packed things into your boxes.
Callum: Could've done, actually. We do a lot of food stuff, outer cases mostly.
Debbie: I always liked it, you know, getting into a rhythm on the line, and the girls were lovely. I just couldn't be doing with the forms. I nearly got written up once for forgetting my hairnet three days running.
Callum: Three days! Our lot would've had you in for a chat.
Debbie: Well, I left about two years ago anyway. They changed the shifts, and I mind my grandson now. Do you like your shifts?
Callum: Erm, mostly. Days one week, backs the next. You're knackered by the end of a run of backs, but you get used to it. I'd like to go for shift team leader in a couple of years, maybe.
Debbie: Ooh, good for you. I never wanted to, too much hassle, too many forms. But you'd be good at it, you seem ever so calm.
Callum: Thank you. Yeah, I try not to get rattled. My dad's the same. He drives for a haulage firm, has done for years, but his back's bad now from all that time in the cab, you know.
Debbie: Oh, that's my Steve with his knees. He does removals with his van, and I keep saying to him, you can't be lugging wardrobes at sixty-one forever. He just says, well, who else is going to do it?
Callum: Yeah, that's exactly what my dad says. Word for word, pretty much. I do worry about him, I'll be honest.
Debbie: Course you do, love. That's because you're a good son. My boy's a bit older than you, and you've got the same smile, you have.
Callum: Aw, that's nice. Does he live near you?
Debbie: Ten minutes away. They all do, the whole lot of them. Sorry, I've gone off on one again, I always do. What do you do for fun?
Callum: Five-a-side on Wednesdays, and the garden. I've got tomatoes going, but half of them are still green, so I don't know if they'll make it.
Debbie: Put them in a drawer with a banana, love. That's what my mum always did. Brings them on lovely, that does.
Callum: A banana? Really? Hira said the windowsill, but our cat knocks everything off the windowsill, so a drawer might be the answer.
Debbie: There you go! Out of reach of the cat and all. Do you follow the football? Steve and my son are Norwich mad.
Callum: Gillingham, with my dad. Bit of a rough season, so don't ask.
Debbie: Oh, Norwich are the same, love. Steve shouts at the radio every Saturday, and I just put the kettle on and-

=== CALL C0035 ===
Luke: Hi, Hira, is it? I'm Luke. Third call, we're practically pros now.
Hira: Hello. Yes, Hira. I think so, yes.
Luke: Where are you based?
Hira: Reading. Earley.
Luke: Oh nice, I'm in Bristol, so we're just down the M4 from each other, sort of. I see you've got a lot of books behind you. Are those library ones?
Hira: Some of them. The thick ones are for work. The others are from Reading library.
Luke: What are you reading at the moment? I'm always nosing at people's shelves.
Hira: Erm, a crime novel. A Japanese one, translated. I like translated fiction quite a lot.
Luke: Oh, brilliant, which one? I did a month in Japan a few years ago, so I'm a bit obsessed. I'm forever going on about it, sorry.
Hira: The Devotion of Suspect X. Do you know it?
Luke: Yes! The maths teacher one. That's so good, isn't it, the twist. There's a film of it too, I think, a Korean one as well, maybe. I watch a lot of that stuff at the Watershed here.
Hira: I didn't know there was a film. I'd like to go to Japan one day. Not soon, but one day.
Luke: You should, honestly. Kyoto in the autumn is ridiculous. Anyway, what do you do? Sorry, I've just launched straight into books.
Hira: No, it's fine. I work in a hospital pharmacy. On the wards.
Luke: Oh, wow, that's proper responsibility. I'm an exec assistant, so my big crisis is the MD double-booking a lunch.
Hira: That is also a problem. Just a different kind.
Luke: Ha, thank you, I'll tell him you said that. Do you like it, the hospital?
Hira: Yes. It's a lot of checking, but I like the patients. Many are older, and some only speak Punjabi or Urdu, so I can help with that.
Luke: That must make such a difference for them, being able to actually understand what they're taking.
Hira: Yes, I think so. They relax more.
Luke: Yeah. What do you do to switch off? I do parkrun and I cook, mostly Korean stuff. I make kimchi, which, as Callum's now heard, sometimes explodes.
Hira: Explodes?
Luke: In the jar. Fermentation. It went all up the cupboard and my daughter thought it was the best thing that'd ever happened.
Hira: Ah. Your daughter did the dog drawing, I think. In your photo.
Luke: She did, yeah, Isla, she's nine. She's campaigning for a dog. It's me and her in the week, so a dog feels like a lot right now.
Hira: Yes. It must be a lot already, on your own.
Luke: It is, sometimes, yeah. But she's great. So what about you, walking, anything like that?
Hira: Walking by the river. Swimming on Saturdays. And crochet. I'm slowly making a blanket.
Luke: Crochet's having such a moment, isn't it. There's a little shop in Stokes Croft that does classes. Have you been to any galleries or anything round you?
Hira: Not much. I went to the Ashmolean in Oxford. I enjoyed it more than I expected, actually.
Luke: Oh, that's a good one. I did that years ago with uni mates and we spent forever-

Debbie: Three months! But at least you're still going with it. What colours?
Hira: Grey and mustard. It's for, erm, just for our sofa, I think. Usually I make small things for colleagues when they have babies. Hats, little blankets.
Debbie: Oh, that's ever so kind. They must love that. Where do you work, then, love?
Hira: At the hospital in Reading. In the pharmacy, on the wards.
Debbie: I said you looked clever, with all them big books behind you. I did, I put that on the form.
Hira: They are mostly heavy, not clever.
Debbie: Do you do the old people's wards and that?
Hira: Yes, quite a lot of the medical wards. Many older patients. Later I'd like to specialise in care of the elderly, maybe.
Debbie: Ah. My mum was in and out of hospital at the end. She had dementia. That's five years ago now. The nurses were lovely with her, they really were. I don't know how you all do it, honestly.
Hira: I'm sorry about your mum. Dementia is very hard. For the families especially.
Debbie: That is. Anyway, sorry, love, I'm going all gloomy on you. Where are you from originally, if you don't mind me asking?
Hira: Pakistan. Faisalabad. I came here seven years ago.
Debbie: Seven years! And do you get back much?
Hira: Once a year, normally, for two or three weeks. My parents are there, and one sister. I talk to my sisters on video at the weekends. Sometimes my sister sends voice notes at three in the morning, our time.
Debbie: Oh, that's the time difference, isn't it! My sister's only round the corner, so she just turns up. I've got nearly all my family within a few miles, you know. I'd be lost without them. Do you miss your mum?
Hira: Yes. More than I say, I think. Mostly I miss her cooking. I'm still trying to make my chapatis as round as hers.
Debbie: Oh, bless you. Mine would come out the shape of Norfolk. What do you cook, then?
Hira: Daal, aloo gosht, mostly Punjabi food. And on Sundays a roast chicken, because my mother-in-law likes it.
Debbie: Ooh, a roast! Do you do Yorkshires?
Hira: Erm, I tried once. They didn't rise. Na, they were flat.
Debbie: That's the oven, love. You want it ever so hot, and the oil smoking before the batter goes in. That's the secret, that is. My Steve won't have a Sunday without them.
Hira: Okay. Very hot. I'll try that. Thank you.
Debbie: And don't open the door! That's where everybody goes wrong, they peek.
Hira: I think I peeked.
Debbie: Everybody does, love. Do you walk at all? I take Tilly, my dog, along the seafront every day. She's got a bad hip, but she still drags me out.
Hira: Yes, I walk by the river on the Thames Path, or round the lake near us. It's nice when it's not raining, which is not often.
Debbie: Oh, the wind off the sea here, that'd take your-
calls.C0033:
Luke: Hey, Callum, is it? I'm Luke.
Callum: Yeah, that's me. Alright, mate, nice to meet you.
Luke: You too. Where are you?
Callum: Sittingbourne, in Kent. You?
Luke: Bristol. So there's a bit of motorway between us.
Callum: Bit of a trek, yeah. Is that a Studio Ghibli thing behind you? My wife's been on at me to watch one of those.
Luke: It is, yeah, Spirited Away. Oh, you've got to. Start with that one, honestly, or My Neighbour Totoro if you want something gentle. I've got a nine-year-old and she's watched Totoro about forty times.
Callum: Right, I'll tell Megan. She'll be chuffed I've actually remembered something. What do you do, then?
Luke: I'm an exec assistant to the MD at an engineering consultancy. Basically I run his life: diary, board meetings, travel, suppliers. And you?
Callum: Machine operator. Cardboard boxes. I run a flexo printer-folder-gluer, so the board goes in flat and comes out a box, printed and glued. I do the changeovers as well when an order switches. Days one week, backs the next.
Luke: That's actually quite satisfying, isn't it? Like, you can see the thing at the end.
Callum: Yeah, that's it, you can see what you've done. I train the new starters and all, which I quite like. I'm trying to get on the maintenance apprenticeship, so I can fix the machines rather than just run them, you know.
Luke: Oh, nice. That's a smart move. I'm sort of in the same boat, trying to work out the next step. Chief of staff, head of ops, that kind of thing. The trick is making yourself the person nobody can do without, yeah?
Callum: Yeah, I suppose. I just try and do the job properly and hope someone notices.
Luke: That works too, to be fair. Probably more honest than mine. Do you do much sport?
Callum: Five-a-side on Wednesdays with lads from work. I'm at the back, mostly, just stopping people getting through. And I go to Gillingham with my dad now and then.
Luke: Gillingham! I'm Rovers, sort of by inheritance from my dad. I take my daughter a couple of times a season. I'm more of a parkrun person, really. Horfield Common, when she's at her mum's.
Callum: Oh, what do you get round in?
Luke: Erm, on a good day, just under twenty-four. On a bad day I'd rather not say.
Callum: That's decent, that. I'd be dead. I do a bit of cycling on the Saxon Shore Way, but that's about it.
Luke: What do you do when you're not knackered from shifts?
Callum: Garden, mostly. I built raised beds out the back. Tomatoes, chillies, runner beans. I was just talking chillies with Hira in the last one, actually. She grows them too.
Luke: Ha, nice. I make kimchi, so I'm always after chillies. Well, the flakes, gochugaru. My last batch sort of exploded in the jar.
Callum: Exploded?
Luke: Fermentation. The gas builds up. I opened it and it went all up the cupboard. Isla thought it was the best thing ever.
Callum: That's mental. I'm just chilli and fajitas, me. And a kebab on a Friday from the place by the station.
Luke: Honestly, a good kebab's hard to beat. Where've you been on holiday lately? I'm always nosing.
Callum: Lads' weekend in Newcastle last time. And me and Megan do Norfolk or Devon in the summer, a cottage or a caravan. Honeymoon was Crete. I like it all booked and sorted, you know, so nothing goes wrong.
Luke: Oh, you'd be good at my job, then. I did a month in Japan before my daughter came along, and I'm desperate to do Seoul next, but-
calls.C0034:
Debbie: Hello, love! Ooh, it's you. I said you looked lovely in your photo. I'm Debbie.
Callum: Ha, thank you. Hiya, Debbie, I'm Callum. You alright?
Debbie: I'm fine, love, thank you. Bit worn out with all this talking, I'm not used to it. Where are you, then?
Callum: Sittingbourne, in Kent. Whereabouts are you?
Debbie: Gorleston-on-Sea. Right by Great Yarmouth.
Callum: Oh, no way, we come up to Norfolk most summers, me and my wife. Caravan or a cottage. We did one near Hemsby a couple of years back.
Debbie: Hemsby! That's just up the road, love. Did you get fish and chips on the front?
Callum: Pretty much every night. Megan was like, we can't have chips again, and then we had chips again.
Debbie: That's what you're supposed to do on holiday, that is. We have them every Friday, me and my husband Steve, and we live here.
Callum: Ha. Fair enough. Did you get on alright with the puzzle at the start?
Debbie: Oh, don't. The dog started barking halfway through and I lost my place. What do you do, love?
Callum: I'm a machine operator. I run a printer-folder-gluer at a cardboard box factory. The board goes in flat and comes out a box, basically.
Debbie: Oh, I did packing for years! Frozen food, near Yarmouth. I bet I've packed things into your boxes.
Callum: Could've done, actually. We do a lot of food stuff, outer cases mostly.
Debbie: I always liked it, you know, getting into a rhythm on the line, and the girls were lovely. I just couldn't be doing with the forms. I nearly got written up once for forgetting my hairnet three days running.
Callum: Three days! Our lot would've had you in for a chat.
Debbie: Well, I left about two years ago anyway. They changed the shifts, and I mind my grandson now. Do you like your shifts?
Callum: Erm, mostly. Days one week, backs the next. You're knackered by the end of a run of backs, but you get used to it. I'd like to go for shift team leader in a couple of years, maybe.
Debbie: Ooh, good for you. I never wanted to, too much hassle, too many forms. But you'd be good at it, you seem ever so calm.
Callum: Thank you. Yeah, I try not to get rattled. My dad's the same. He drives for a haulage firm, has done for years, but his back's bad now from all that time in the cab, you know.
Debbie: Oh, that's my Steve with his knees. He does removals with his van, and I keep saying to him, you can't be lugging wardrobes at sixty-one forever. He just says, well, who else is going to do it?
Callum: Yeah, that's exactly what my dad says. Word for word, pretty much. I do worry about him, I'll be honest.
Debbie: Course you do, love. That's because you're a good son. My boy's a bit older than you, and you've got the same smile, you have.
Callum: Aw, that's nice. Does he live near you?
Debbie: Ten minutes away. They all do, the whole lot of them. Sorry, I've gone off on one again, I always do. What do you do for fun?
Callum: Five-a-side on Wednesdays, and the garden. I've got tomatoes going, but half of them are still green, so I don't know if they'll make it.
Debbie: Put them in a drawer with a banana, love. That's what my mum always did. Brings them on lovely, that does.
Callum: A banana? Really? Hira said the windowsill, but our cat knocks everything off the windowsill, so a drawer might be the answer.
Debbie: There you go! Out of reach of the cat and all. Do you follow the football? Steve and my son are Norwich mad.
Callum: Gillingham, with my dad. Bit of a rough season, so don't ask.
Debbie: Oh, Norwich are the same, love. Steve shouts at the radio every Saturday, and I just put the kettle on and-
calls.C0035:
Luke: Hi, Hira, is it? I'm Luke. Third call, we're practically pros now.
Hira: Hello. Yes, Hira. I think so, yes.
Luke: Where are you based?
Hira: Reading. Earley.
Luke: Oh nice, I'm in Bristol, so we're just down the M4 from each other, sort of. I see you've got a lot of books behind you. Are those library ones?
Hira: Some of them. The thick ones are for work. The others are from Reading library.
Luke: What are you reading at the moment? I'm always nosing at people's shelves.
Hira: Erm, a crime novel. A Japanese one, translated. I like translated fiction quite a lot.
Luke: Oh, brilliant, which one? I did a month in Japan a few years ago, so I'm a bit obsessed. I'm forever going on about it, sorry.
Hira: The Devotion of Suspect X. Do you know it?
Luke: Yes! The maths teacher one. That's so good, isn't it, the twist. There's a film of it too, I think, a Korean one as well, maybe. I watch a lot of that stuff at the Watershed here.
Hira: I didn't know there was a film. I'd like to go to Japan one day. Not soon, but one day.
Luke: You should, honestly. Kyoto in the autumn is ridiculous. Anyway, what do you do? Sorry, I've just launched straight into books.
Hira: No, it's fine. I work in a hospital pharmacy. On the wards.
Luke: Oh, wow, that's proper responsibility. I'm an exec assistant, so my big crisis is the MD double-booking a lunch.
Hira: That is also a problem. Just a different kind.
Luke: Ha, thank you, I'll tell him you said that. Do you like it, the hospital?
Hira: Yes. It's a lot of checking, but I like the patients. Many are older, and some only speak Punjabi or Urdu, so I can help with that.
Luke: That must make such a difference for them, being able to actually understand what they're taking.
Hira: Yes, I think so. They relax more.
Luke: Yeah. What do you do to switch off? I do parkrun and I cook, mostly Korean stuff. I make kimchi, which, as Callum's now heard, sometimes explodes.
Hira: Explodes?
Luke: In the jar. Fermentation. It went all up the cupboard and my daughter thought it was the best thing that'd ever happened.
Hira: Ah. Your daughter did the dog drawing, I think. In your photo.
Luke: She did, yeah, Isla, she's nine. She's campaigning for a dog. It's me and her in the week, so a dog feels like a lot right now.
Hira: Yes. It must be a lot already, on your own.
Luke: It is, sometimes, yeah. But she's great. So what about you, walking, anything like that?
Hira: Walking by the river. Swimming on Saturdays. And crochet. I'm slowly making a blanket.
Luke: Crochet's having such a moment, isn't it. There's a little shop in Stokes Croft that does classes. Have you been to any galleries or anything round you?
Hira: Not much. I went to the Ashmolean in Oxford. I enjoyed it more than I expected, actually.
Luke: Oh, that's a good one. I did that years ago with uni mates and we spent forever-

C0034.line_text: Yeah, that's exactly what my dad says. Word for word, pretty much. I do worry about him, I'll be honest.
C0034.what: Callum glances down at the table and lets out a slow breath, pausing for about a second before saying 'I do worry about him', his half-smile dropping briefly before it comes back.
